Statement : The blocking of BitChat's code on GitHub is unconstitutional and authoritarian. 

New Delhi, 24 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the order issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, directing GitHub to remove the code repositories of BitChat. 

The order, Notice No. 11072601011432, was issued at 11:16 pm on 23 July 2026 under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021. The order directs GitHub to disable access to three repositories, including the Android application and its release files, within three hours. It threatens the platform with loss of safe harbour and criminal prosecution. No copy was published by the Government of India. The public learnt of it from a post by @jack, whose team develops BitChat. Censorship in India now comes to light through disclosure by the censored.

Since 17 July 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs has suspended mobile internet around Jantar Mantar as per public reports about five times, most recently within a 1.5 kilometre radius from 4 pm until midnight on 23 July. That radius takes in Janpath and parts of Connaught Place. Reports describe signal jammers at the protest site and people walking two kilometres before their phones work. Inside that zone a student separated from her group during a detention drive cannot send a message to say where she is. Thousands of students and young people have camped at Jantar Mantar since June, seeking accountability for examination irregularities. Permission for their march to Parliament was refused. Metro stations were shut and also internet connectivity has been blocked.

BitChat is an open source application built for exactly this situation. It passes messages from phone to phone over Bluetooth, without mobile networks or a central server. It is striking that the order does not identify a single unlawful message. It objects to what BitChat is. In its own words, the application is dangerous because it enables communication "even during network restrictions" and can "circumvent lawful restrictions" during "internet shutdowns". Hence, the government's objection is that citizens can speak to one another while it has switched the internet off. 

The order is illegal on at least four grounds. 

1. Section 79(3)(b) is not a blocking power. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down the provision. Intermediaries may be required to act only on a court order, or a government notification confined to the grounds under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Blocking is governed exclusively by Section 69A and the Blocking Rules, 2009, which require a hearing and reasons recorded in writing, subject to review. Directions issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal evade these safeguards, and constitutional challenges to this parallel regime are pending before High Courts. 

2. The reasons in the order are circular. The order asserts that the repositories contain "information which is prohibited under any law" without naming any such information, and rests on what the application is "capable of" enabling. Anticipated misuse of a communications tool is not a lawful basis to prohibit the tool. By this logic a telephone exchange could be sealed. 

3. The order cites Section 43 of the IT Act, a civil compensation provision, alongside conspiracy and abetment offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, against a platform that hosts code. 

4. A three hour deadline issued close to midnight forecloses legal assessment and recourse, and fails the proportionality standard in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637.

The order also fails on its own terms as deleting a repository does not delete the application from any phone that carries it, and the mesh keeps functioning without servers. What the takedown actually prevents is scrutiny of the underlying code.

IFF demands that the Government of India:

1. Withdraw Notice No. 11072601011432 dated 23 July 2026 issued to GitHub.
2. Publish every takedown direction issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal, with the reasons recorded for each.
3. Restore full connectivity around Jantar Mantar, publish all suspension orders, and disclose the legal authority for the deployment of jammers.

We stand with the developers and the young protesters whose speech this order seeks to silence.

text:
IFF Statement: Blocking of the Cockroach Janta Party's Instagram account

July 22, 2026

The Instagram account of the Cockroach Janta Party (@cockroachjantaparty) is no longer accessible to users in India. Meta's notice states only that it complied with "a legal request to restrict this content". No order has been published and the legal basis, the issuing authority, and the reasons remain unknown.

We emphasise that the account is primarily engaged in acts of political speech that enjoy the full protection of Article 19(1)(a). The account has been restricted after the movement's march to Parliament over the NEET paper leak, and while the Delhi High Court examines allegations of excessive police force against protesters. Viewed in this background the blocking of its social media account at this moment is the suppression of dissent.

The secrecy compounds the illegality. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A of the IT Act on the strength of its procedural safeguards. In Anuradha Bhasin, it held that orders restricting fundamental rights must be published. These safeguards are defeated when the originator learns of a blocking action from an error message.

We also note that Meta's notice refers to a "legal request", not an order.  We call on MeitY to disclose the order, furnish a copy to the account holder, and provide a hearing. We call on Meta to inform the account holder of the specific legal process it received. Wholesale blocking of an entire account is disproportionate and unconstitutional.

text:
Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

text:
Statement on the Indian government's order to GitHub to block BitChat:

The Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (@Cyberdost ) under the Ministry of Home Affairs (@PIBHomeAffairs) has ordered GitHub (@github) to remove three URLs linking to BitChat, an app that works offline without an internet connection and enables users to communicate over Bluetooth. This order was issued under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000, read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021.

During the internet shutdowns imposed on multiple occasions over the past week in parts of Central Delhi, many protesters faced difficulties communicating or seeking emergency services. Open-source applications like BitChat allow people to communicate with other people using the same application nearby, without an internet connection.

The order states that the application would impede the state's ability to conduct lawful interception and surveillance and enable users to circumvent lawful restrictions such as internet shutdowns. The notice was issued at 11:16 PM on 23rd July and has given GitHub three hours to remove the links.

However, the order fails to satisfy the tests of legality, necessity, and proportionality and constitutes as an abject misuse of Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules 2021.

At the outset, Section 79(3)(b) does not confer the power to block or remove content, which instead stems from Section 69A of the IT Act. The issuance of orders with generic grounds is further inconsistent with the safeguards laid down by the Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India. The Supreme Court upheld Section 69A of the IT Act, 2000 strictly because it required that blocking orders must be reasoned, necessary, and proportionate, and that such reasons must be recorded in writing to enable judicial review.

The opacity surrounding these removals goes against the strict requirements of accountability and record-keeping embedded in the Information Technology (Procedure and Safeguards for Blocking for Access of Information by Public) Rules, 2009.

The only reason this particular order in the current instance became public is not due to dissemination by the issuing authority, but rather because @Jack posted about the same on X. What we see emerging through these removals is a system of informal, decentralised censorship, where the government can direct content removals without transparency or oversight.

The lack of information renders a meaningful legal challenge impossible and leaves affected parties without legal redressal, including the basic elements of review that Section 69A provides when read with the Blocking Rules 2009. Orders passed under Section 79(3)(b) therefore function as circumventions of the procedural safeguards enumerated under Section 69A of the IT Act.

text:
The Delhi Police's takedown drive against posts critical of the Prime Minister is unconstitutional. 

New Delhi, 27 July 2026

Media reports today state that the Delhi Police has directed social media platforms to remove posts, videos, memes and reels containing remarks it describes as "abusive", "offensive" and "objectionable" towards the Prime Minister, uploaded during the student protests at Jantar Mantar and after the 'Sansad Chalo' march of 20 July 2026. At least three platforms have reportedly received notices. Several posts have already been taken down. A dedicated police team is monitoring social media to identify further content, and reports indicate that criminal proceedings are contemplated against those who posted it. No order has been published. While reports indicate the notices invoke the Information Technology Act, the specific provision relied upon and the text of the notices remain undisclosed. 

The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns this takedown drive and calls for the notices to be disclosed and withdrawn.

On the reports available, the content being removed is political expression. The movement at Jantar Mantar has been conducted as much through reels, memes, posters and digital artwork as through assembly on the ground. This is how a digital native generation raised online speaks about accountability. As per Article 19(2) restrictions on speech only on eight specified grounds. Offensiveness is not one of them. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the IT Act precisely because expressions such as "grossly offensive" and causing "annoyance" were vague, subjective, and swept protected speech within their net. Eleven years later, the Delhi Police is applying the same standard through informal notices and legal powers which are not being publicly disclosed. 

As per existing practices there are two routes for removing online content. The first is Section 69A of the IT Act read with the Blocking Rules, 2009, which requires a reasoned order, committee review, and notice to the originator, as the Delhi High Court affirmed in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). The second is Section 79(3)(b), which Shreya Singhal read down to require a court order or a government notification strictly confined to Article 19(2) grounds. If these notices were routed through the Sahyog Portal, they rest on a regime whose constitutionality remains under challenge before multiple High Courts. However, even if it is used police notices citing offensiveness satisfy neither. 

Reports that platforms were told the content violates "their policies" make the defect worse, the police have no mandate to enforce the community guidelines of private companies. Unpublished directions are also contrary to Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637, which requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published so that they can be challenged. If the underlying theory is defamation of the Prime Minister, the police have no role at all. Defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognizable offence, prosecuted only on a complaint by the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. 

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must publish every notice issued, the legal provision invoked, and the list of URLs affected.

2. Notices directed at satire, criticism, and political commentary must be withdrawn. Any removal must follow the procedures under Section 69A or a judicial order.

3. No criminal proceedings should be initiated against persons for speech that does not meet the constitutional threshold of incitement.

4. Platforms must decline requests unsupported by valid legal orders, notify affected users, and disclose the number of government demands in their transparency reports.

Students who question an examination system are exercising their fundamental rights and deleting their posts will not delete their questions.

Reports referred to:

1. Times of India, "Delhi Police orders removal of offensive posts against PM Narendra Modi linked to NEET paper leak protests", 27 July 2026
2. News18, "Delhi Police Issues Notices To Social Media Platforms Over Offensive Posts Against PM Modi During Jantar Mantar Protest", 27 July 2026

The X account of David Peterson (@davidgpeterson), General Manager at @ProtonVPN, has been suspended in India.

This came after he posted about a 150% surge in hourly registrations for Proton VPN from India, following @telegram's temporary ban in the country.

Proton VPN is a virtual private network (VPN) service that allows users to change their apparent online location. By using a VPN, people in India could route their internet traffic through servers outside the country and access blocked platforms such as Telegram.

The suspension of his account adds to the growing trend of content takedowns and account suspensions ordered without transparency.

Most of these orders are being issued under Section 69A of the IT Act, which allows the government to issue blocking orders on broad grounds such as national security or public order.

Read with Rule 16 of the Information Technology (Procedure and Safeguards for Blocking Access of Information by Public) Rules, 2009, this provision requires confidentiality regarding all requests and complaints received as well as actions taken.

As a result, the person facing information blocking may never be heard or provided a reasoned order on why their content is blocked online. Apart from causing a chilling effect on free speech, this violates basic tenets of natural justice.

text:
IFF statement against the Alarming Escalation of Social Media Censorship and Proposed Expansion of Takedown Powers

New Delhi, March 19, 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by continuing reports of posts and accounts being withheld in India on Facebook, X and Instagram, including satire and criticism of the government. Recent reporting shows users receiving generic “withheld in India” notices or emails under Section 69A from social media platforms, with little or no explanation, while independent reporting has documented takedowns affecting speech that appears political, satirical, or critical rather than clearly unlawful.

As reported by Business Standard and The Indian Express on March 18, the Union Government is currently exploring a proposal to decentralize content blocking powers under Section 69A of the IT Act. The new proposal would grant direct takedown powers to multiple ministries, including Defence, Home Affairs, External Affairs, and Information & Broadcasting. At present, MeitY signs off on Section 69A orders, while a separate notice and takedown channel already operates through Section 79(3)(b) and the Home Ministry led Sahyog portal that at least has 35 nodal officers across State Police Departments in India.

At the same time, the February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules have sharply compressed compliance timelines. MeitY’s own published FAQ says intermediaries must act within 3 hours when they receive actual knowledge through a court order or a government intimation, within 36 hours for certain expedited grievances, and within 2 hours for specified complaints involving nudity, sexual content, morphed content, and impersonation. The government has also reiterated that intermediaries which fail to observe due diligence risk losing Section 79 immunity. A system built on speed, legal threat, and secrecy predictably incentivises over compliance.

We remind the Union Government that the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A in the Shreya Singhal case on the basis of procedural safeguards and written reasons that could be challenged. Secret and inaccessible censorship defeats those safeguards in practice. 

IFF calls on the Union government to halt any move to decentralise Section 69A blocking powers further, publish blocking orders with only as per the letter and spirit of the Shreya Singhal judgement, and ensure timely notice to affected users with clear grounds and avenues for remedy. Platforms must also do more than send boilerplate messages. They should provide meaningful notice, preserve records for challenge, and publish granular transparency reporting given online censorship also impacts the public right to receive information.

If your account or post has been withheld or blocked in India, please write to legal@internetfreedom.in with screenshots, URLs, and any email or platform notice you have received. IFF will try to assist impacted users and document patterns of opaque censorship.

Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

THREAD 🧵 | Why the Supreme Court’s order regarding Imran Khan’s medical treatment can be defended through existing Pakistani precedents

If the Government files a Review Petition, Imran Khan’s legal team can rely on the following precedents. Not every case is identical, but together they establish important principles concerning medical bail, prisoners’ constitutional rights, State duty of care and judicial protection.

1/10 — Muhammad Yousafullah Khan v. The State — PLD 1995 SC 58
The Supreme Court recognized medical grounds as a basis for bail where the required treatment cannot adequately be provided in custody and continued detention may seriously affect the prisoner’s health.
This is one of the key authorities for the medical-bail test.

2/10 — Muhammad Saeed Mehdi v. The State — 2002 SCMR 282
Bench: Justice Muhammad Bashir Jehangiri, Justice Rana Bhagwandas & Justice Munir A. Sheikh.
The Supreme Court granted bail where the accused required immediate treatment, hospitalization and close monitoring by specialists in a properly equipped hospital.
The Court held that such treatment could not be achieved simply by keeping the person in custody and sending him to hospital only for limited treatment.
This is highly relevant to the argument that specialist treatment must actually be available, not merely theoretically accessible.

3/10 — Peer Mukaram-ul-Haq v. NAB — 2006 SCMR 1225
Bench: Justice Javed Iqbal & Justice Abdul Hameed Dogar.
The Supreme Court considered medical evidence showing that the required specialists and facilities were not available in the local hospital and granted bail.
The judgment is important because the Court looked at the actual availability of specialised medical facilities, rather than merely accepting that some basic treatment existed.

4/10 — Nawaz Sharif — Al-Azizia medical-bail case, March 2019
The Islamabad High Court had rejected medical relief, but the Supreme Court intervened and granted Nawaz Sharif six weeks’ bail on medical grounds and suspended his sentence.
Bench:
Chief Justice Asif Saeed Khan Khosa
Justice Sajjad Ali Shah
Justice Yahya Afridi
This precedent is particularly important because it demonstrates that the Supreme Court can independently examine medical evidence and grant appropriate relief even after a High Court has refused it.

5/10 — Mst. Safia Bano v. Home Department — PLD 2021 SC 488
The Supreme Court dealt extensively with mentally ill prisoners, medical assessment, Medical Boards, treatment and the humane administration of punishment.
The case supports the broader constitutional principle that imprisonment does not erase a prisoner’s fundamental rights or the State’s responsibility toward the prisoner’s health and humane treatment.

6/10 — Raja Azmat Ali v. Abu Malik Naseem — 2023 SCMR 1867
Bench: Chief Justice Umar Ata Bandial & Justice Athar Minallah.
This is one of the strongest prisoner-rights precedents.
The Supreme Court held that a prisoner — whether convicted or under trial — remains entitled to constitutional protection of life, dignity and fair treatment.
The Court emphasized that incarceration curtails liberty and freedom of movement, but does not extinguish fundamental rights. Because prisoners depend upon the State for protection of life, health and humane treatment, the State owes them a duty of care.
This is directly relevant to defending constitutional protection for Imran Khan.

#Constitution #ImranKhan #SupremeCourt #RuleOfLaw

7/10 — Shehla Zia v. WAPDA — PLD 1994 SC 693
Bench:
Chief Justice Nasim Hasan Shah
Justice Saleem Akhtar
Justice Manzoor Hussain Sial
The Supreme Court gave Article 9’s Right to Life a broad constitutional interpretation.
Although this was not a prisoner case, it provides an important constitutional foundation for arguments concerning protection of life, health and human safety.

8/10 — Muhammad Hussain v. The State — Peshawar High Court, https://t.co/1EKMQS3eG3 No. 3743-P/2020
The Peshawar High Court applied the established medical-bail principles where serious illness, the need for specialised treatment and the availability of adequate treatment in custody were relevant considerations.
This is particularly relevant because it is a High Court authority applying the medical-bail test in practice.

9/10 — Khawar Kayani v. The State — PLD 2022 SC 551
Crl.P. No. 345/2022 — Supreme Court of Pakistan
This case concerns statutory bail and the interpretation of the Juvenile Justice System Act rather than medical treatment.
It should therefore not be presented as a direct medical-bail precedent. Its value is in the broader principle that statutory provisions governing custody and bail must be interpreted according to the protective purpose of the law.

10/10 — Tahira Batool v. The State — PLD 2022 SC 764
Crl.P. No. 910/2022 — Supreme Court of Pakistan
The Supreme Court discussed the scope of the first proviso to Section 497(1) Cr.P.C. and emphasized that statutory exceptions to the normal bail framework must be properly considered.
Again, this is not a direct medical-transfer case, but it can be relevant when lawyers argue that statutory bail provisions should be interpreted according to their protective purpose.

CONCLUSION

The Legal Argument for Imran Khan
Taken together, these authorities provide several important lines of argument:
• Medical evidence matters.
• A prisoner does not lose constitutional rights merely because he is incarcerated.
• The State owes prisoners a duty of care regarding life, health and humane treatment.
• Where specialised treatment is required, the question is whether that treatment is actually available, not merely whether a basic prison medical facility exists.
• The Supreme Court has previously intervened on medical grounds even after a High Court refused relief.
• Prison Rules provide an administrative mechanism, but they cannot automatically extinguish constitutional protections under Articles 9 and 14.
The strongest authorities for the present issue are:
Nawaz Sharif (2019) — medical relief after IHC refusal
Muhammad Saeed Mehdi (2002 SCMR 282) — specialist hospital treatment
Peer Mukaram-ul-Haq (2006 SCMR 1225) — availability of specialised facilities
Safia Bano (PLD 2021 SC 488) — Medical Boards and prisoner health
Raja Azmat Ali (2023 SCMR 1867) — prisoner’s life, dignity and State duty of care
Shehla Zia (PLD 1994 SC 693) — constitutional protection of life
Therefore, the Government cannot simply argue:
“Prison Rules give the executive authority, therefore the Supreme Court had no power to intervene.”
The real question is whether the constitutional jurisdiction of the Court can be exercised where a prisoner’s life, health and dignity are at stake.
The above jurisprudence provides a substantial legal basis for arguing that it can.
The law must apply equally to every prisoner — including Imran Khan.

#ImranKhan #SupremeCourt #RuleOfLaw #Justice #Pakistan

She Works Full Time. Day Care Costs More Than Her Rent.
Single mothers in America, by the numbers — and the one experiment that proved we know how to fix it

Let's start with a number that I had to check three times because I assumed I'd misread it.

Put an infant and a four-year-old in a child care center in America. In every single state we have data for — all 47 of them — that costs more than the median rent. Not a comparable amount. More.

In 39 states it costs more than a median mortgage payment. Infant care alone costs more than in-state public college tuition in 38 states.

Now think about who's paying that. For a two-parent household, child care eats about 10 percent of median income. For a single-parent household: 33 percent. A third of everything, before rent, before food, before anything.

And here's the part that makes it a trap rather than just an expense. If she quits to care for the kids, she has no income. If she works, a third of her income goes to the care that lets her work. There's no version of that math that comes out clean.

Where this ends up

Nearly 31 percent of families with children headed by a single woman were living in poverty. The national poverty rate is about 10.6 percent.

That's not double. It's roughly three times.

Break it down further and it gets worse. For families with children headed by a single Latina woman, it's around 37 percent. For families headed by a single Native or Indigenous woman, closer to 39 percent.

On food: 36.8 percent of households headed by a single woman with children were food insecure — meaning at some point in the year they had trouble getting enough food. The national household rate is 13.7 percent. Again, nearly three times.

I want to flag something about that food number before we go on, because it matters. That figure comes from a federal survey that has now been discontinued. The report it came from was the last edition. There will be no comparable national measurement going forward — which means we've stopped counting hunger right as we started cutting food aid. Hold that thought.

The thing America doesn't have

The United States has no federal paid maternity leave. None. Not reduced, not partial. It doesn't exist.

What exists is the Family and Medical Leave Act, from 1993, and it's unpaid. It also has three eligibility gates: your employer must have 50 or more employees, you must have worked there 12 months, and you must have logged 1,250 hours in the past year. About 44 percent of workers can't clear those bars.

And even for the ones who can — it's unpaid. Which for a single mother is the same as not existing.

Now the number that tells you exactly who this hits. Among the lowest-paid 10 percent of workers, how many have employer-provided paid family leave?

Six percent.

Among the highest-paid 10 percent? Forty-three.

So the people most likely to lose everything from an unpaid month off are the people least likely to be offered a paid one. That's not a gap in the system. That's the shape of the system.

Fifteen states and D.C. have built their own paid leave programs. Which means whether a woman can afford to recover from childbirth depends on which state line she happens to live inside.

The single-parent penalty nobody wrote down

Here's one I only found because I went looking at the actual statute.

A budget law passed in July 2025 expanded work-reporting requirements for food assistance. It now reaches parents of children 14 and older — previously, parents were exempt until their youngest turned 18.

Now watch the mechanics. In a married couple, only one parent has to meet the requirement. The other one can be the one picking up the kid.

A single mother has to be both people. She has to meet the work requirement and be the one who's there when school ends. There is no second adult to absorb it.

Roughly two million more women are newly subject to those rules. About 80 percent of single-parent households are headed by mothers.

Since that law took effect, food assistance participation has fallen by more than 4.5 million people — about 11 percent in nine months, the steepest drop the program has ever had. More than 1.5 million of them are children. Unemployment stayed flat the whole time. People didn't stop needing it.

We already ran the experiment

This is the part I keep coming back to, because it takes the whole thing out of the realm of opinion.

In 2021, the child tax credit was temporarily expanded and made fully refundable — meaning families too poor to owe income tax could still receive it in full.

Child poverty fell to 5.2 percent. The lowest ever recorded.

The expansion expired. One year later, child poverty was back at 12.4 percent — more than double. It was the largest single-year increase for children in data going back to 1967.

Up, then down, in twenty-four months, tracking one policy. You almost never get evidence that clean in social policy. We ran the experiment, it worked, and we stopped.

The credit that exists today is $2,200 per child. But because it still isn't fully refundable, roughly 60 percent of children with a single female parent don't qualify for the full amount — because their family doesn't earn enough. Read that again. The child benefit phases in with income, so the poorest children get the least.

Two things people will say, and they're worth answering

"What about child support?"

Fair question. Answer: only about 43 percent of custodial parents owed child support receive the full amount. Roughly a quarter receive nothing at all. Custodial-mother families have a poverty rate around 27 percent; custodial-father families, around 11 percent. Child support is real, it matters, and it does not fill this hole.

"Marriage is the answer."

This is the serious conservative argument and it deserves a serious response rather than an eye-roll.

The claim, roughly: finish high school, work full time, marry before having children — do those three in that order and you're dramatically less likely to be poor. Married-couple families are poor at a fraction of the rate of single-mother families. Two adults means two potential earners and two people who can handle a sick kid.

The descriptive part of that is just true, and pretending otherwise is dishonest.

Here's where I think it breaks. The research is descriptive, not causal — a federal literature review looking at it concluded causation isn't established. When you decompose it, full-time work is doing most of the anti-poverty lifting, not the wedding. And the direction of the arrow is genuinely unclear: economic precarity is one of the best predictors of relationships not forming or not lasting. Telling a woman working two jobs with no paid leave and a day care bill bigger than her rent that her problem is she didn't marry first isn't a policy. It's a preference.

Also, and this is the practical objection: "get married" isn't something a government can hand out. Refundable tax credits are.

While we're clearing things up

A couple of numbers get thrown around in this debate that are wrong or sloppy, and I'd rather correct them myself than have someone correct me.

"Women earn less for the same work." Two different measurements get jammed together here. Women working full time year-round earn about 81 cents for every dollar men earn — that's the real, raw gap and it's been widening. But when you control for the same job, same hours, same experience, it's about 99 cents. Which means the big gap isn't mostly "same job, less pay." It's women concentrated in lower-paying occupations, working fewer paid hours, and taking the hit for having kids. That's arguably a bigger problem, but it's a different problem, and calling it the wrong thing is how you lose the argument.

Single mothers aren't who the stereotype says. They're divorced, separated, widowed, and never-married, in meaningful numbers across all four. The teenage-mistake caricature describes a slice, not the population.

And roughly three million mothers work in the forty lowest-paid occupations in the country — child care workers, home health aides, waitresses, cashiers — earning sixteen dollars an hour or less. Including, and I find this genuinely absurd, the women being paid poverty wages to look after other people's children.

One housekeeping note, because it's part of the story

Most of the poverty and hunger figures here are from 2024. That's not laziness — it's the lag. The Census surveys households about last year's income and publishes in September.

Which means the 2025 numbers land this September, and they'll be the first to capture the food-assistance cuts. When they arrive, these figures need updating.

If they arrive on schedule. The hunger survey has already been discontinued. A related annual release currently has no publication date while a new Commerce Department order on statistical disclosure is being assessed. And the federal statistics office recently had to re-issue several years of poverty thresholds after finding coding errors.

I'm not alleging anything. I'm saying: keep an eye on whether the numbers show up. A country that stops publishing how many of its children are hungry hasn't fixed anything.

So what do you actually think?

I've laid out what I found. Here's where I genuinely want to hear from you.

If a working mother's day care bill is larger than her rent, is that a personal budgeting problem or a market failure?

We have the receipts on the 2021 credit — poverty halved, then doubled back. If a policy demonstrably works and costs money, what's the argument against it that isn't just "it costs money"?

And the one I keep chewing on: the child benefit phases in with income, so the poorest children get the smallest amount. Is there a defensible reason for that, or is it just how the sausage got made?

Tell me what I've got wrong. I'd rather fix it than defend it.

Thesis: NTRPY (@0xNTRPY) — Entropy as On-Chain Ritual: Generative Transformation, Philosophical Permanence, and Community Emergence on Robinhood Chain

Abstract

NTRPY (pronounced “entropy”), the project behind the X account @0xNTRPY, is a 3,333-piece free-mint generative NFT collection launching on Robinhood Chain on August 20, 2026 (2 PM EST via OpenSea). It reframes entropy—not as mere thermodynamic decay or disorder, but as “the turning within” (from Greek en + tropē)—into a fully on-chain system of chrome animal forms generated deterministically from 64-character hashes. Through cryptic “trials,” alchemical motifs, and interactive transformation mechanics, the project treats NFTs as living processes rather than static assets. This thesis argues that NTRPY exemplifies a mature evolution in generative art and crypto culture: it prioritizes philosophical coherence, technical permanence, and participatory ritual over hype cycles, turning community engagement itself into an emergent order arising from intentional chaos.
1. Introduction and Project Overview
@0xNTRPY presents itself with the bio: “NTRPY (“entropy”). chaos seeking form, order emerging from disorder.” The account (joined December 2022, ~22.5k followers as of mid-August 2026) functions less as a conventional project page and more as a ritual vessel. The website (https://t.co/2BOe3JCxIn) frames the work as “an archive of transformation” consisting of chrome-rendered animals suspended in void. Chrome has no color of its own—it reflects its surroundings—making each piece a mirror of context rather than a fixed image.

Key parameters (drawn from official posts, community deep-dives, and project materials):
Supply: locked at 3,333.

Price: free.
Chain: Robinhood  Chain
Generation: fully on-chain, deterministic from a unique 64-character hash seed. The same seed always regenerates the identical form.

Team signals: Founder @deepxhl (crypto builder since 2017); creative/coding contributions linked to @JustJay4k.

Mint phases emphasize fairness (BAYC holders noted for early access/delegation; WL via content, trials, and engagement rather than pure capital). The project explicitly rejects common NFT failure modes: “Dead metadata. Dead servers. A wallet nobody opens with a broken link inside it. The chain held up fine. The people didn’t.”

2. Philosophical Core: Entropy Reclaimed
Classical entropy (Clausius, 1865) quantifies the irreversible increase in disorder or “transformational content.” Popular culture often reduces it to heat death or chaos. NTRPY recovers the original sense of entropē as an inward turning—dissolution as the precondition for higher organization.

The collection catalogs eight mechanisms of change (some community sources note six primary + rarities), each embodied as a specimen type:

Psyche (Metamorphosis): total dissolution and internal rebuilding (the butterfly/soul).
Ouroboros (Ecdysis): shedding; “you go blind right before you see clearly.”

Proteus (Mutability): refusal of fixed form.
Arachne (Self-construction): building structure from one’s own substance.
Glaux (Casting): expelling what will not dissolve.
Ketos: reversion / going backward.
Skorpios (Refusal): ultra-rare stasis (<0.5% in some reports).
Theoria (Witness): transformation through being observed.
Alchemical stages (nigredo → albedo → citrinitas → rubedo) and the motto solve ✦ coagula reinforce the motif. Order is “paid for”; the only thing that survives dissolution is the image of what one is becoming. This is not decorative lore—it structures the art, the mint mechanics, and the social layer.

3. Technical and Artistic Architecture
Unlike pre-rendered collections that point to IPFS or centralized servers, NTRPY generates forms live via compact on-chain code (reports cite ~5 KB engines using techniques such as signed distance fields, raymarching, and smooth-minimum blending). The artwork is the generative rule itself; the visible chrome creature is its temporary manifestation. This achieves genuine permanence: decades later, the same hash still yields the identical piece.
Some descriptions position the NFTs as dynamic/larval at mint, capable of further evolution through interaction, with rarity earned rather than assigned at genesis. Burnability and future “chapters” are signaled. In a post-2021 NFT landscape saturated with static JPEGs and metadata decay, this is a deliberate corrective—entropy made computable and self-sustaining.

4. Social and Ritual Layer: Cult Mechanics as Emergent Order
@0xNTRPY cultivates a “cult” aesthetic (👁️ motif, “fellow cult members,” cryptic field notes). “Trials” function as progressive puzzles (Vigenère ciphers, visual overlays, Minesweeper-style challenges later scrapped for fairness after extreme demand). Solving yields words that unlock the next stage; answers are DMed under strict single-entry rules to deter Sybils. Content contests reward genuine engagement over “AI slop.” Spaces, articles, and collaborative posts amplify the mystery.

This is not accidental. By distributing access through intellectual and creative labor rather than pure capital or follow-for-follow, the project engineers participation as a dissipative structure—local order arising from broader informational chaos. Community members become co-authors of the narrative, mirroring the generative process itself.
5. Contextual Significance on Robinhood Chain
Robinhood Chain launched as an RWA-focused L2 (tokenized stocks, self-custody, 24/7 markets) yet rapidly attracted memecoins and early NFT experiments. NTRPY arrives amid this open phase as one of the more conceptually ambitious drops: free, fully generative, philosophically dense, and timed for maximum cultural signal. It tests whether a chain designed for financial democratization can also host durable artistic and communal experiments.

6. Argument and Implications
NTRPY’s thesis-in-action is that true permanence in digital art requires both technical on-chain fidelity and cultural mechanisms that treat holders as carriers rather than owners (“You don’t hold something that’s already coming apart. You carry it for a while and hand it to whoever’s next”). By embedding entropy’s dual nature—dissolution as generative force—into code, aesthetics, and community design, the project models a post-speculative NFT paradigm. Success will be measured less by secondary volume than by whether the 3,333 forms continue to regenerate, transform, and invite new seekers years after the mint.

Limitations remain: pre-mint status means long-term dynamics (actual evolution mechanics, secondary market behavior, team execution) are unproven. The cryptic style risks alienating casual participants even as it filters for committed ones. Yet in an ecosystem still recovering from cycles of overpromise and metadata rot, NTRPY’s insistence on the one promise it can keep—fixed supply, deterministic generation, philosophical consistency—stands as a rigorous, self-aware intervention.
Conclusion
@0xNTRPY is not merely another generative collection. It is a working demonstration that chaos, properly ritualized and encoded, can produce durable form. In reclaiming entropy as “the turning within,” the project invites participants to undergo the same process the art depicts: dissolution of prior assumptions about what an NFT is, followed by the emergence of something more resilient. Whether the chrome animals ultimately reflect a lasting cultural order or dissolve into the next cycle will itself be an empirical test of the thesis they embody.

(Primary sources: @0xNTRPY and associated accounts’ posts and X articles, https://t.co/2BOe3JCxIn conceptual materials, community analyses, and Robinhood Chain context as of August 2026.)

text:
Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

The Three-Pronged Squeeze of Such Moves by Governments

1. Taxation as Pressure

Print: 5% GST on newspapers, but digital subscriptions at 18%—asymmetry makes bundling difficult .

Newsprint duty: Industry still pays 5%, despite calls for full removal to ease rising costs .

Government ad rates for digital publishers dropped 50-60% in four years—serious news competes with inventory-flooding platforms .

2. The Three-Hour Rule
New IT Rules (effective Feb 2026) require platforms to remove content within 3 hours of government notice (down from 36) .
Legal experts: This forces "remove first, review later"—automated censorship, not judgment .

Satire, parody, political commentary get swept up .

Supreme Court's Shreya Singhal framework (requiring specificity) arguably inverted .

3. Data Act & RTI Amendment
Digital Personal Data Protection Act amended RTI's Section 8(1)(j) :

Before: PIOs could disclose personal info if "larger public interest" justified it.
Now: Absolute exemption for "personal information"—no public interest override .

Petitioners in Supreme Court argue this shields corrupt officials, cripples investigative journalism .

Journalists now potentially "data fiduciaries"—need consent from those they investigate .

Bottom line: 
Tax squeezes economics. Timelines force pre-emptive removal. Data law seals information. Three tools, one outcome.

text:
Bad becomes worse? Further changes proposed to the proposed changes to IT Rules!

Today, post-noon on 21 April 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has published further proposed amendments to the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Second Amendment Rules, 2026.

The notice states that these are limited to Rule 3(3)(a)(ii) requiring that labels identifying synthetically generated information be continuously and clearly visible throughout the duration of the content in visual display. This goes beyond the earlier requirement of “prominent” visibility, and now mandates persistent, uninterrupted disclosure for the entire duration of such content. This requirement is applicable to all users of social media and AI tools, and not just digital news platforms.

All other provisions in the newly updated draft remain the same as the draft circulated on 30 March 2026. Our comments to the MeitY are available here. The consultation timeline has now been extended allowing stakeholders to submit comments on both the earlier draft amendments and these additional amendments by 07 May 2026. We note that suggesting changes within the window of a pre-existing public consultation process in which thousands of Indians have voiced opposition is likely to result in, “consultation fatigue” and at the very least demonstrates a pattern of ad-hoc policy making than one which accounts for structured and planned feedback.

Further, MeitY has once again indicated that the submissions will be held in fiduciary capacity in MeitY and shall not be disclosed to any one at any stage, enabling persons to submit feedback/comments freely without any hesitation. Importantly, consultation processes are important for democratic decision making, placing the responses in the public domain would ensure meaningful engagement and participation by stakeholders. It would also allow for better analysis, understanding, and fair critique of the various perspectives put forward. We therefore urge MeitY to place the comments and feedback on their website in the interest of democracy and transparency.

We urge citizenry to participate in such public consultation and share their feedback/comments on the draft rules in a rule wise manner by email to itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in in MS Word or PDF format by 07th May, 2026. We have drafted a short template email which readers can improvise upon.

As of today, more than 4500 people have used our link to improve upon and send their own comments to MeitY primarily asking for a withdrawal of the proposed changes to the IT Rules, 2021.

text:
"Digital India" can process billions of UPI transactions, authenticate Aadhaar in seconds, deploy facial recognition, and run databases at population scale.

But ask the MEA a basic question: how many passports have been issued to non-citizens?

The reply: "We do not maintain consolidated data."

That answer raises a bigger question than the number itself.

Passport issuance today is a digital workflow. Applications generate electronic records. Identity and supporting documents are captured. 

Decisions are recorded. Passports are issued against individual files. 

In any properly designed database, producing an aggregate from structured records is exactly what a simple query is meant to do.

So, what does "we do not maintain consolidated data" actually mean?

Does the underlying information not exist in structured form?

Is it fragmented across systems that cannot be queried together?

Is citizenship or nationality not stored in a reliably searchable field?

Or does the government have the data but simply not compile or retrieve the aggregate?

These are very different explanations, and the public deserves a clear answer.

This matters because passports are not a minor administrative detail. 

The Passports Act explicitly deals with nationality and non-citizenship. 

If the State cannot readily determine, from its own passport system, how many documents fall into a legally significant category, that is a serious issue of data design, auditability, and institutional accountability.

And if the information can be generated from existing digital records but is still not being produced, then a harder question follows:

Is this a technical limitation, or a decision not to look?

Before celebrating "Digital India", we should ask something more basic:

Can the government interrogate its own databases when the public asks a legitimate question?

Because digitization without retrievability is just electronic filing.

And databases without accountability are not Digital India. They are digital opacity.

🚨 Digital State + New Laws in Sri Lanka: A Perfect Storm Threatening Civic Space

At least seven laws and draft bills enacted or circulated in Sri Lanka since 2023, combined with the rapid construction of a digital state, create a credible capacity to intimidate, incapacitate or criminalise dissent without declaring an emergency, warns researcher Sanjana Hattotuwa.

These instruments include the Online Safety Act, Anti-Corruption Act, Proceeds of Crime Act, the proposed Protection of the State from Terrorism Act (PSTA), the draft NGO Registration and Supervision Bill, and cybersecurity measures. Alongside them, the government is building a unique digital identity, national data exchange, upgraded government cloud, digital payments and a single public-services app. Human rights receive little attention in the accompanying AI and sovereign cloud strategies.

News Analysis;

The real danger lies not in any single clause but in the "interaction design" of these laws and digital systems working together. The Personal Data Protection Act remains only partly in force until January 2027, while the digital architecture hardens between 2026 and 2028 - before the next election. The Executive Presidency remains the terminus for key appointments and powers. Historical precedent (the use of voter lists against Tamil households in 1983) shows how digitisation removes earlier friction. Hattotuwa correctly argues that international funders, including the World Bank and UN agencies, should treat rights safeguards as conditions of disbursement rather than accompanying language. Weak safeguards and unequal enforcement make the risks especially severe for civil society and minority communities.

An article claims that Meta has automated content blocking to comply with the government's three-hour takedown requirement, and that content blocks surged during the #Delhiprotests.

#PIBFactCheck: 

❌ The article is #Misleading. 

✅ To expedite action against unlawful content, the takedown time was reduced to 3 hours from earlier 36 hours by an amendment in February 2026 to the IT Intermediaries Rules 2021.

Zig when others zag?  Not really, just have integrity and do the right thing.

In the last 5 months we’ve unseated multiple Indian engineering companies because our clients don’t want to talk to a guy in India.  My clients refuse to talk to Chinese robot suppliers.

Now, the 232 tariff on robotics has dropped.  The FCC banned foreign autonomous robots.  And more actions are in the pipeline.  We have a hard earned pipeline of AMERICAN suppliers and they give us preference on pricing and lead times.  Today, talent and lead time wins the game. 

My American engineers keep referring their American friends to come work at @ChangRobotics.  The universities we recruit at roll out the red carpet and refer the best students ahead of the career fairs.  They subsidize our lab spaces.
