GoDaddy has challenged a Delhi High Court order that it says could reshape how the internet works far beyond India.

In December, the court blocked more than 1,100 fake websites impersonating brands like Amazon, McDonald's and Microsoft. But the ruling went further, issuing 14 directives that tech experts say rewrite the rules of internet governance. Domain sellers can no longer offer free privacy protection by default. A website owner's name, address, phone and email must be released to anyone with a "legitimate interest" within 72 hours. Domain names resembling protected brand names are prohibited outright.

GoDaddy, which manages 80 million domains for over 20 million customers, has filed a 5,121-page appeal arguing the order conflicts with India's own data protection law and the EU's GDPR. It warns the directives are commercially destabilising enough to force domain companies to exit India. Namecheap and Hosting Concepts have filed their own challenges.

India's concern is grounded in a real crisis. The government received 2.4 million cybercrime complaints last year involving losses of 2.4 billion dollars, and the Home Minister has said one person falls victim to cybercrime every 37 seconds. Court records show the directives closely followed submissions by the IT and home ministries.

Internet governance researchers warn the people exposed by public registration data will be journalists, activists and small business owners rather than fraudsters. GoDaddy points to a practical problem: protecting a trademark like HUL would overlap with 118 English words, including hulk and moghul.

A larger bench hears the appeals on July 16. A domestic anti-fraud ruling is quietly becoming a global internet governance precedent.

Source: Reuters

Appeal लेट, The End नहीं
Delay माफ, merits की राह खुली

● ● ●

⭐ आज की बात
नमस्ते दोस्त!

कभी 𝗚𝗦𝗧 में असली लड़ाई tax demand से पहले limitation की हो जाती है। Shiva Steelage के सामने भी यही मुश्किल थी—FY 2018-19 के लिए ₹30,51,323 की 𝗜𝗧𝗖 demand थी, लेकिन statutory 𝗔𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗮𝗹 समय पर file नहीं हो पाई।
Taxpayer का कहना था कि Order-in-Original केवल 𝗣𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗮𝗹 पर upload हुआ; e-mail, SMS या certified copy से effective communication नहीं हुआ। वह CA और accountant पर compliance के लिए dependent था और order व appeal limitation से समय पर अवगत नहीं हुआ।

● ● ●

⭐ विवाद कहाँ अटक गया?
Order-in-Original 04.05.2024 का था। Taxpayer ने यह भी दलील दी कि order ex parte था और effective Personal Hearing नहीं मिली।

लेकिन बड़ी procedural रुकावट यह थी कि इतनी delay को Appellate Authority 𝗦𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝟭𝟬𝟳(𝟰) के बाहर condone नहीं कर सकती थी। इसलिए मामला High Court पहुँचा।

● ● ●

⭐ दोनों पक्षों का stand
Petitioner ने कहा कि delay जानबूझकर नहीं थी और circumstances उसके control से बाहर थे। Department ने writ oppose करते हुए कहा कि impugned order सही था और appeal अब limitation से barred है।

● ● ●

⭐ Court ने किस बात पर ध्यान दिया?
Court ने 𝗜𝗧𝗖 की correctness तय नहीं की। उसने यह देखा कि क्या limitation के कारण taxpayer को merits पर सुनवाई से पूरी तरह वंचित करना, बताए गए circumstances में, grave prejudice पैदा करेगा।

Court ने Rajasthan High Court के earlier decisions का consistent view देखा और Punjab & Haryana High Court के Luxmi Traders judgment से भी सहमति जताई, जिसमें portal-only service और delayed appeal जैसी स्थितियों पर relief का framework discussed था।

● ● ●

⭐ इस Judgment का Crux Point
इस case की निर्णायक बात यह थी कि statutory appellate limitation अपनी जगह थी, फिर भी High Court ने facts और delay के कारणों को देखते हुए procedural दरवाज़ा बंद नहीं रहने दिया।

यानी relief का मतलब 𝗗𝗲𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗱 खत्म होना नहीं था; केवल 𝗺𝗲𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘀 पर appeal सुनने की राह खुली।

● ● ●

⭐ Judgment में किन Legal References का इस्तेमाल हुआ?
📂 𝗦𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝟭𝟬𝟳 और 𝗦𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝟭𝟬𝟳(𝟰) appellate limitation के संदर्भ में महत्वपूर्ण रहे। Court ने माना कि Appellate Authority statutory limit से बंधी है।

📚 Rajasthan High Court ने M/s M R Traders v. UOI, M/s Molana Construction Company v. Central Goods and Service Tax Department & Ors., Man Singh Tanwar v. Commissioner, CGST Department & Ors. और RPC PSIPL JV के earlier decisions का consistent approach refer किया, जहाँ delayed appeals को merits पर entertain करने की दिशा दी गई थी।

📚 Luxmi Traders v. Union Territory of Chandigarh & Ors. में Punjab & Haryana High Court के portal-only service संबंधी view से Rajasthan High Court ने respectful agreement जताया। इसी background ने petitioner को procedural relief देने की reasoning को support किया।

● ● ●

⭐ आखिर Court ने क्या किया?
High Court ने delay condone की और Appellate Authority को appeal entertain कर 𝗺𝗲𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘀 पर adjudicate करने का निर्देश दिया—लेकिन condition के साथ।

✅ Appeal High Court का order website पर upload होने के 30 days के भीतर file करनी होगी।

⚠️ ₹30,51,323 की demand quash नहीं हुई, 𝗜𝗧𝗖 entitlement decide नहीं हुई और taxpayer को merits पर final clean chit नहीं मिली।

● ● ●

⭐ चलते चलते
इस judgment की practical सीख limitation tracking की है।

1️⃣ GST Portal और communication trail को नियमित monitor करें।
2️⃣ Adverse order मिलते ही appeal deadline note करें।
3️⃣ Delay हो जाए तो facts, communication और procedural record को संभालकर रखें।

यह फैसला हर late appeal के लिए automatic relief नहीं बनाता; इसका दायरा facts और Court द्वारा स्वीकार किए गए circumstances से जुड़ा है।

● ● ●

it comes down to three stages:

① build a foundation Google and AI can crawl and understand
② attract visitors with useful content
③ use data to turn those visitors into signups and purchases

ranking on Google isn’t enough.

if AI engines can’t understand your content—or visitors land on your site but don’t understand the value—you still won’t get results.

the key is identifying which stage is broken and improving it with a clear goal.

if you want to improve your website or grow your organic traffic, bookmark this.

1. Understand What’s Happening With Data

the first step is making sure you can see what is actually happening.

not guesses. real data.

the two main tools you need are Google Analytics 4 (GA4) and Google Search Console (GSC).

both are free.

GA4 shows what people do after they visit your website:

・which pages get the most traffic
・whether visitors come from Google, social media, or other channels
・whether visitors come from AI tools like ChatGPT or Perplexity
・which pages lead to signups or purchases

Google Search Console shows how people discover you through Google:

・which keywords your pages appear for
・how many people click from search results
・your average search position
・which articles are gaining or losing rankings

with these two tools, you can separate two very different problems:

“not enough people are visiting”

vs.

“people are visiting, but they aren’t taking action”

connect GA4 and Google Search Console to NoimosAI, and it can analyze the data and suggest what to improve.

feed these prompts into NoimosAI to identify the room for improvement:
“Analyze traffic from Google Search and AI search engines using GA4 and GSC, then recommend the pages with the highest improvement potential.”

“Using GSC data, identify articles that have lost rankings and recommend which ones should be rewritten.”

2. Build a Technical Foundation Google and AI Can Understand

you can create the most useful content in your industry.

but if Google and AI can’t properly crawl and understand it, people won’t find it through search results or AI-generated answers.

here’s what to check:

・are your important pages indexed by Google?
・does your sitemap tell crawlers which pages exist?
・is robots.txt accidentally blocking Google or AI crawlers?
・does the site load quickly and work well on mobile?
・are there broken links or layout issues?
・does JSON-LD clearly identify your company, products, and articles?
・does llms.txt organize your most important pages for AI?

robots.txt, sitemaps, and JSON-LD create a shared technical foundation for both traditional search and AI search.

the work that helps Google discover and understand your pages is called technical SEO.

GEO goes one step further by making your content easier for AI engines to understand and use in their answers.

NoimosAI can analyze page speed, site structure, robots.txt, JSON-LD, and other technical issues—then recommend improvements for both search engines and AI.

use this prompt in NoimosAI to optimize your site:
“Audit [Website URL] for search engine and AI readability. Analyze robots.txt, the sitemap, JSON-LD, llms.txt, and page speed, then recommend specific improvements.”

3. Communicate Your Value Above the Fold

visitors decide within seconds whether they want to keep reading.

the first screen they see should answer three questions:

・who is this for?
・what problem does it solve?
・what should I do next?

listing dozens of features won’t help if visitors can’t see why the product matters to them.

for example, describing NoimosAI as “a powerful AI agent” is too abstract.

“delegate your marketing work to AI” makes the outcome much easier to understand.

don’t just describe the product.

show people what changes after they use it.

prompt to find the best messages for your site:
“Analyze the first screen visitors see on [Website URL], then suggest a headline and supporting copy that communicate the value immediately.”

4. Give People a Reason to Trust You and Take Action

interest alone doesn’t create signups.

even when people understand your service, they may still wonder:

“does this actually work?”

“will this work for my company?”

your website needs to answer those questions with evidence.

use things like:

・real product screenshots
・specific use cases
・customer results
・testimonials
・supported integrations
・security information
・pricing and the steps required to get started

don’t add everything just to make the page longer.

choose the proof that addresses the biggest concerns customers have before signing up.

on the NoimosAI website, we show the product, supported services, customer testimonials, and security information before guiding visitors toward getting started.

5. Choose Keywords That Can Generate Revenue

once the foundation is ready, you need to attract the right visitors.

a better website won’t generate results if nobody sees it.

start with the problems your customers are already searching for on Google.

then create articles that solve those problems and introduce your product as one possible solution.

the key: don’t target a keyword just because it has high search volume.

for example, “best AI tools” may get a lot of searches, but it is extremely competitive.

more specific keywords like:

“best AI tools for social media posts”

or:

“best AI tools for competitor analysis”

usually have clearer intent and less competition.

use data from Semrush or similar tools to find keywords that:

・match a real problem your customers have
・have enough search volume to matter
・aren’t dominated by impossible competition
・show comparison, evaluation, or purchase intent

a good keyword doesn’t just generate traffic.

it attracts people who could eventually become customers.

use this prompt to find the best keywords to get visitors:
“Find keywords that customers of [Product or Service] are searching for. Organize them by search volume, ranking difficulty, and search intent.”

6. Create Articles That Rank on Google and Get Understood by AI

once you choose a keyword, analyze the pages already ranking for it.

top-ranking pages reveal what people are expecting to find.

but copying the same information gives people no reason to read your article.

first, analyze the SEO side:

・what topics appear across most top-ranking articles?
・what order makes the information easiest to understand?
・what information is missing?
・what information is outdated?
・where can you add your own experience or data?

then make the structure easy for AI to understand:

・answer one clear question under each heading
・give the direct answer first
・summarize the most important points
・include examples, numbers, and sources
・add an FAQ at the end

don’t write an FAQ that avoids the question.

answer it directly in the first one or two sentences, then explain the reasoning and examples.

this makes the article easier for readers to scan and easier for AI to extract useful answers from.

that’s a core part of GEO.

NoimosAI can analyze Google search results, create the article structure, write the content, and include summaries, direct answers, and FAQs designed for both SEO and GEO.

prompt:
“Analyze the top-ranking search results for [Keyword], then create an SEO/GEO-optimized article targeting that keyword.”

7. Use Data to Find What to Improve

publishing a page is not the finish line.

algorithms change. information becomes outdated. customer behavior changes.

you need to keep improving based on what the data tells you.

the same “underperforming page” can have completely different problems:

・high search impressions, but few clicks
　→ the title or description isn’t compelling enough

・high rankings, but little traffic
　→ the keyword may have low search demand

・high traffic, but few signups
　→ the content, CTA, page flow, or trust signals may be weak

・an article used to perform, but rankings dropped
　→ the information may be outdated, or competitors may now offer better content

don’t try to fix every page at once.

identify the cause, then start with the pages where a small improvement could create the biggest result.

prompt to use in NoimosAI:
“Using GSC and GA4, categorize pages into: ① pages that don’t appear in search, ② pages that appear but don’t get clicked, and ③ pages that get traffic but don’t generate signups. Recommend improvements for each.”

8. Compare Before and After, Then Keep Improving

website optimization is never a one-time project.

when you change a title, check the click-through rate.

when you update an article, check its search ranking.

when you change the page structure, check the signup rate.

record every change and compare the numbers before and after.

that’s how you learn which improvements are actually driving results.

here’s what we review every month:

・pages gaining or losing search impressions
・pages gaining or losing traffic from ChatGPT, Perplexity, and other AI services
・pages with low click-through rates
・articles losing rankings
・high-traffic pages that don’t generate signups
・pages with speed issues
・traffic sources generating signups or purchases

we use NoimosAI agents to continuously identify keyword gaps and rewrite underperforming content.

feed these prompts into NoimosAI to find the gap between you and your competitors:
“Every week, identify high-priority keywords that competitors rank for but we don’t, then create one new article idea.”

“Every month, compare the latest 28 days with the previous 28 days. Use search rankings, clicks, and traffic from AI services to identify the article with the highest improvement potential and create a rewrite plan.”

website optimization isn’t about launching a flashy redesign.

it’s about:

・building a system that measures results
・making your value easy to understand
・creating content around real customer problems
・improving continuously based on data

repeat this process, and your website stops being a static company brochure.

it becomes a system that consistently generates customers.

Steps to fix it ⬇️

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
ANDROID

iPHONE / iPAD

Wi-Fi only (iOS limitation):
1. Settings → Wi-Fi → tap (i) next to your network
2. Configure DNS → Manual
3. Remove existing entries
4. Add 1.1.1.1 and 1.0.0.1
5. Save

For mobile data: install the "1.1.1.1: Faster Internet" app by Cloudflare from App Store. It sets up a system-wide profile.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
WINDOWS 11 / 10

1. Settings → Network & Internet → Wi-Fi (or Ethernet)
2. Click your active connection
3. Scroll to "DNS server assignment" → Edit

5. Preferred: 1.1.1.1 | Alternate: 1.0.0.1
6. Save

Press Windows key → type "cmd" → right-click "Command Prompt" → Run as administrator → Yes. Black window opens. Type ipconfig /flushdns, press Enter.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
macOS

1. System Settings → Network
2. Click your active connection → Details
3. Click DNS in sidebar
4. Click + and add 1.1.1.1, then 1.0.0.1
5. Remove existing ISP entries (select, click −)
6. OK → Apply

Open Terminal: press Cmd + Space → type "Terminal" → Enter. Copy-paste sudo dscacheutil -flushcache; sudo killall -HUP mDNSResponder, press Enter, type your Mac password (invisible while typing, that's normal), press Enter.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
ROUTER (covers every device on Wi-Fi)

1. Open 192.168.1.1 or 192.168.0.1 in browser
2. Login (credentials usually on router sticker)
3. Find DNS settings (under WAN, Internet, or DHCP)
4. Primary: 1.1.1.1 | Secondary: 1.0.0.1

Best option if you want laptop + phone + smart TV + everything to work without per-device setup.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

*STATEMENT: Escalating Digital Censorship in India*

*New Delhi, February 28, 2026*

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by a cluster of online blocking and takedown actions and ISP level service disruptions reported between 24–28 February 2026. Across these incidents, users and affected services face restrictions without clear, timely reasons and without access to the underlying orders needed to challenge state action by exercising their rights to obtain legal remedy.

Developers reported severe, uneven disruption in access to Supabase across multiple Indian networks. Reporting indicates the disruption followed a government direction, with accounts suggesting use of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Yet there has been no public statement of the grounds, scope, or duration, and no accessible order for those impacted. Supabase has publicly stated that its domains became inaccessible due to a “ministry order”, and users have been pushed to workarounds such as alternative DNS or VPNs. In parallel, users on X (formerly Twitter) continue to receive “withheld in India” notices restricting specific posts within the country. Such notices usually do not provide the government order or its reasoning. Hence, for those who are being censored the basics of natural justice of a notice, opportunity for a hearing and remedy are delayed or absent.

This is enabled by secrecy built into the blocking framework. Section 69A is implemented through the 2009 Blocking Rules, which contemplate a committee process and, where feasible, notice to intermediaries and identifiable originators. But they also impose “strict confidentiality” over requests and actions taken. When orders and reasons are secret by default, affected persons cannot test legality, necessity, proportionality, or factual errors except through protracted litigation. When in _Shreya Singhal v. Union of India_ (2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A while relying on the existence of procedural safeguards and reasoned decisions, indicating that impacted users could approach court in writ remedies. However, due to the operational secrecy and providing copies of orders and notices those who are censored and prevented from obtaining judicial remedy.

The February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules, 2021 further increase these risks. The substituted Rule 3(1)(d) requires intermediaries to remove or disable access within three hours of receiving “actual knowledge”, which can arise from a court order or a written “reasoned intimation” by authorised government officers. While the rule lists what a “reasoned intimation” should contain, the legal basis, statutory provision, nature of the unlawful act, and specific URL/identifier, the three-hour window pressures platforms to comply promptly which may often occur without any substantive assessment. These inherently opaque censorship practices are being accelerated through "Sahyog" portal. Developed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the Sahyog portal operates entirely without statutory footing, only being anchored in the IT Rules, 2021 that are created by executive notification. It functions as a censorship clearinghouse that deliberately bypasses the established, albeit weak, procedural safeguards of Section 69A. By routing automated takedown directives directly to intermediaries under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, the portal structurally excludes citizens and impacted users from the grievance process.

We demand that the government introduce strictly judicially enforceable transparency requirements, publish all blocking orders, and restore the principles of natural justice to India's platform governance framework. Based on requests from our community we will also next week launch a rough public sheet in which social media users can input and add information on digital censorship.

Clear difference between Brazil and India on X regard to the open source X:

🇧🇷 Brazil • Type: Hardcoded filter in the open-source algorithm • What it is: Public ranking rule written into the code (Brazil2026ElectionFilter) • Visibility: Fully visible and inspectable in the GitHub repo • Effect: Affects “For You” recommendations (unless you already follow the account) • Scope: Official election-related candidate/campaign accounts (~665 TSE-listed for 2026)

Brazil’s election law requires platforms that use recommendation systems to treat official candidate accounts this way. X implemented it as transparent, auditable code.

🇮🇳 India • Type: Individual legal requests / orders • What it is: Case-by-case legal notices (mainly Section 69A of the IT Act) • Visibility: Specific notices and lists are mostly confidential under Indian law • Effect: Usually withholds content only inside India • Scope: Any content the government deems a threat to sovereignty, security, or public order

India has no equivalent hardcoded ranking filter in the open-source algorithm. It relies on traditional legal takedown/withholding orders.

Filters (hardcoded in open-source X algorithm) → Currently only Brazil (Brazil2026ElectionFilter)
Requests (government content removal / withholding demands)
 These are standard legal notices. X reviews them and publishes aggregate numbers in its Transparency Reports.

Highest volume (H2 2024 data from the 2025 Transparency Report): • Japan — by far the largest (69,186). Mostly local criminal laws (fraud, “yami-baito” recruitment, drugs, prostitution) • Turkey — 11,107 • South Korea — 1,835 • European Union (combined) — 3,831 • All other countries (including India, Brazil, Russia, etc.) — 11,047 combined

India is a significant requester under Section 69A and the IT Rules. X publishes separate monthly compliance reports for India, but the individual orders remain largely confidential. Content is typically withheld only for users in India.

Other regular requesters include Russia, Indonesia, Malaysia, and various EU states. None currently have a Brazil-style public filter in the open-source recommendation code.

Summary • Filters = Brazil only (visible in the code) • Requests = Many countries, with Japan, Turkey, South Korea, and India among the more active. These are handled through the normal legal process + aggregate transparency reporting, outside the open-source algorithm.

USA on X: Government Requests – Current vs Pre-Elon

🇺🇸 Current (post-Elon X, H2 2024 / 2025 Transparency Report)
 • Type: Almost entirely information/account-data requests (subpoenas, court orders, emergency disclosures). Formal content removal/withholding orders are rare. • Visibility: Aggregate numbers published in Transparency Reports. Individual requests often notified to users (unless legally prohibited). No hardcoded ranking filter in the open-source algorithm.
 • Volume: – Information requests: 3,788 (highest single country), 2,975 disclosed (78.5% rate) – Removal/withholding requests: Not broken out separately — sits inside “All Others” (~11,047 combined across dozens of countries). Japan alone accounts for ~69,000.
 • Effect: Content is almost never geo-withheld solely because the US government asks. Actions happen mainly for clear illegal content under US law or X’s own rules.
 • Scope: Criminal investigations, national security process, court orders. First Amendment sharply limits government ability to demand pure content takedowns.
Pre-Elon (Twitter, 2019–2021 reports)
 • Information requests: Also frequently the top single country (examples: ~3,026 in H1 2021 ≈ 24% of global volume, ~68% compliance; H2 2021 ≈ 20% of global, ~69% compliance). Volumes in the same ballpark as today.
 • Removal/legal demands from the US: Consistently low volume (often dozens or low hundreds at most per half-year). Global removal totals were lower overall (~40–47k per half-year).
 • Content moderation frequently involved informal government flagging and pressure (documented in the Twitter Files — FBI and other agencies routinely sent “requests” or flagged content for review under Twitter’s TOS, outside formal legal process).
Key differences (current vs pre-Elon)
 • Formal US removal/withholding volume: Remained low in both eras (First Amendment constraint).
 • Global context: Total worldwide removal requests roughly doubled post-acquisition, driven almost entirely by non-US countries (Japan, Turkey, etc.). Overall compliance rates on formal requests rose (~70–82% vs ~30–50% range pre-Elon).
 • Transparency & process: Pre-Musk had regular reports but significant informal channels. Post-Musk: reports resumed after a gap, open-sourced algorithm (only Brazil currently has a public government-required ranking filter), stronger user-notification policy, public challenges to some overbroad foreign orders, and stated rejection of secret deals.
 • Internal moderation: Pre-Elon heavier proactive enforcement on political, COVID, and election-related speech under broad TOS policies. Current approach is narrower (“freedom of speech, not reach”).

Summary The USA is the opposite of Brazil (hardcoded public ranking filter) and India (high-volume confidential Section 69A-style withholding).
 • High activity on information/data requests (stable volume, somewhat higher formal disclosure rate now).
 • Very low activity on formal content removal requests (both pre- and post-Elon).
 Main shifts under X: greater formal transparency, reduced informal pressure channels, and open visibility of any systemic ranking rules when they exist.

Sources: X 2025 Transparency Report (H2 2024 data), historical Twitter Transparency Reports (2019–2021), and public Twitter Files disclosures.

Amid heightened tensions and a heavy police presence in Jaipur, the capital of Rajasthan state in India, the local administration has begun demolishing a 44-year-old historic mosque. The operation was carried out on Sunday (June 7) to remove the historic Noorani Mosque, located in the Malviya Nagar area of Jaipur.

The four-story Noorani Mosque located in Malviya Nagar, Jaipur, India, is being demolished by the authorities as part of a road-widening project. In connection with the operation, internet services across the city were suspended for 24 hours, and extensive security measures were put in place.

The Jaipur Development Authority (JDA) claims that the mosque was constructed illegally on leased land. However, the mosque committee has rejected this allegation, stating that the land was legally purchased from a housing society in 1981 before the structure was built.

A large number of police personnel have been deployed in and around the area, drone surveillance is being conducted, and restrictive orders remain in effect throughout the operation. The mosque committee and several opposition lawmakers have criticized the move, alleging that proper procedures were not followed.

Authorities stated that the temporary internet shutdown was imposed to prevent the spread of rumors and misinformation and to maintain law and order during the demolition process. So far, the operation has remained peaceful, with no reports of violence or unrest.

Statement : IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. No suspension order has been made public.

New Delhi, 20 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services imposed today, 20 July 2026, in parts of Central Delhi, including the area around Jantar Mantar. The shutdown coincided with the 'Chalo Sansad' march called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on the opening day of the Monsoon Session of Parliament, where thousands of students and young people had gathered to press their demands. Permission for the march was refused. Prohibitory orders were imposed under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. Routes to Parliament were sealed, and metro stations including, Patel Chowk, Rajiv Chowk and Janpath were closed. Amid reports of the use of force to disperse protesters, mobile internet was then switched off, reportedly "as a precautionary measure". We urge the immediate restoration of all telecommunication services in the capital and an end to internet shutdowns across India.

The developments of today are of immense consequence to the future of our democracy. The voices gathered at Jantar Mantar, and the residents of the national capital, need to be heard the loudest, not silenced en masse.

No order has been made public

At the time of release of this statement, no copy of any suspension order has been published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. Residents of the capital do not know which authority directed the shutdown, on what grounds, over which precise areas, for which services, or for what duration. An unpublished order is an unaccountable order. It cannot be challenged before a court, and the judicial review guaranteed by the Supreme Court becomes illusory. Some reports further indicate the deployment of network jammers in parts of Central Delhi, including near Jantar Mantar. Jamming equipment finds no sanction in the legal framework for the suspension of telecommunication services at all. If jammers were deployed, the government must disclose under what legal authority.

Binding safeguards violated

On 10 January 2020, the Supreme Court in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637 held that the freedom of speech and expression, and the freedom to carry on trade or business through the medium of the internet, are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The Court directed that every order suspending telecom services must be published. Reasons must be recorded in writing. The restriction must be proportionate, adopting the least restrictive measure available. It cannot continue indefinitely. It is subject to judicial review, and to scrutiny by a review committee.

Parliament has since replaced the framework of the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023, telecommunication services may be suspended only on the occurrence of a public emergency or in the interest of public safety, on the grounds specified in that provision, and for reasons recorded in writing. The Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, notified on 22 November 2024, give effect to this power. A suspension order may be issued only by the Union Home Secretary or the State Home Secretary. An officer not below the rank of Joint Secretary may act in unavoidable circumstances, subject to confirmation by the competent authority within twenty four hours. Every order must clearly define the geographical area and the specific services suspended, and cannot remain in operation beyond fifteen days. Every order must also be published. A Review Committee must meet within five days of the order and record its findings on whether it complies with Section 20(2).

These safeguards are not being followed

If we account for today's shutdown against this legal architecture. The order is unpublished, in breach of Anuradha Bhasin and the Suspension Rules, 2024 alike. No recorded reasons are available to the public despite little to no reports of violence and consistent calls for the protest to be peaceful by the CJP and other organisers. The precise areas and services covered are undisclosed and so is the duration. Whether the competent authority even issued the order cannot be known. Whether the Review Committee will examine it cannot be verified. While the Suspension Rules prescribe no outer time limit for publication, a gap we have previously flagged, it cannot cut against the spirit of the Anuradha Bhasin judgement. A blanket suspension across densely populated parts of the capital, imposed as a "precaution" against a march to Parliament, is the opposite of a narrowly tailored, least restrictive measure. A shutdown timed to a protest restricts the freedoms of speech and assembly at the very moment they matter most.

The human cost of a shutdown

Access to the internet is a digital right on which the exercise of our fundamental freedoms now depends. When the network goes dark in Central Delhi, a journalist at Jantar Mantar cannot file her report or broadcast live. A street vendor on the surrounding roads cannot accept a UPI payment. A gig worker loses a day's earnings. A parent cannot confirm that a child who joined the march is safe. Cutting off communications prevents people from reaching out for help and manufactures panic in a moment which demands calm. These costs fall hardest on daily wage earners and small traders who can least absorb them. Internet based communications also promote trust between people and their government. 

A pattern, not an aberration

Delhi has seen this before. On 19 December 2019, mobile services were suspended for the first time in the capital's history during the protests against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, in areas including Seelampur, Jamia Nagar and Mandi House. On 26 January 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs suspended internet services in Singhu, Ghazipur, Tikri, Mukarba Chowk, Nangloi and their adjoining areas during the farmers' protests. According to the #KeepItOn coalition's report released in March 2026, India recorded 65 internet shutdowns in 2025, the highest of any democracy in the world, and accounts for 920 of the 2,102 shutdowns documented globally since 2016. We have consistently advocated against the harm these disruptions cause, from Jammu and Kashmir to Rajasthan, and from Haryana to Manipur, where a shutdown in 2023 ran for over two hundred days. The orders are rarely published on time, and the findings of review committees never see daylight.

Our demands

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore all suspended telecommunication and internet services in Central Delhi.
2. Publish forthwith every suspension order passed on or around 20 July 2026, together with the reasons recorded in writing, as mandated by Anuradha Bhasin and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024.
3. Disclose the issuing authority, the grounds, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation, and clarify whether network jammers were deployed and under what legal authority.
4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days as required by the Rules, and make its findings public.
5. Reform Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 to provide for independent prior authorisation and real consequences for unlawful suspensions.

IFF will file applications under the Right to Information Act, 2005 seeking copies of the suspension orders and the records of the Review Committee, and is examining further legal remedies. 

Delhi and all of India deserve better.

🤔Timelines, Patterns, Bilateral Deals & One Signature. Three Gates.

On Sunday, the U.S. Treasury published a proposed rule for how stablecoins digital dollars will be regulated in America.

Buried in the legalese is a single clause that connects trade policy, monetary policy, and crypto regulation into one system. Nobody has noticed yet because these things are covered by different reporters on different beats who don't read each other's documents.

Here is the clause, and here is what it means.

The rule

Beginning January 18, 2027, no one may issue a payment stablecoin in the United States without a federal or state license.

Beginning July 18, 2028, no digital asset service provider may offer or sell any payment stablecoin to anyone in the United States unless the coin was issued by a licensed issuer.

That's the domestic side. Every stablecoin Americans can buy must come from a licensed, regulated company. No exceptions.

Now here's the foreign side.

Foreign-issued stablecoins may only be sold to Americans if two conditions are met. First, the foreign issuer must have the technological capability to comply with any lawful U.S. order meaning sanctions screening, freeze orders, law enforcement requests. Second, there must be a reciprocal arrangement between the United States and the issuer's home country.

No reciprocal arrangement, no access to American consumers.

The bilateral deals

Right now, the United States is negotiating bilateral trade agreements with dozens of countries. The 10% baseline tariff from the Section 301 action covers 60 economies. Countries that sign a bilateral deal get their tariff rates negotiated down. Countries that don't sign pay the full rate.

Those deals are being reported as trade policy. Tariffs on goods. Import and export terms.

But read the GENIUS Act rule again.

A country that signs a bilateral agreement with the United States doesn't just get tariff relief. It gets reciprocal arrangement status. That means its financial institutions can issue stablecoins that are legal to sell to Americans. Its payment systems can connect to the U.S. digital dollar market. Its banks, once chartered or licensed, can operate inside the U.S. stablecoin ecosystem.

A country that doesn't sign gets none of that.

The bilateral trade deal and the stablecoin access deal are the same deal. One signature. Three gates: goods, money, and digital currency.

What this means in practice

If you're Japan and you sign a bilateral deal with the United States, your exporters get lower tariffs, your banks can seek stablecoin licenses, and your digital payment systems can interoperate with the American market. You're inside the system for all three.

If you're Iran, there is no bilateral deal, there is no reciprocal arrangement, and your stablecoins your digital currency of any kind cannot legally be sold to an American. Your exchanges get designated by OFAC. Your wallet addresses get published on the sanctions list. You are outside the system for all three.

If you're India and you're at the BRICS summit in September discussing linking your central bank digital currency with China's and Russia's you're simultaneously negotiating a bilateral deal with the United States that would give you access to the world's largest stablecoin market. You can sit at both tables. But the stablecoin access requires compliance with U.S. lawful orders, which means OFAC screening, which means the entire American sanctions architecture applies to your issuers the moment they want to reach American consumers.

You can link your CBDC to Moscow's. But if your bank also wants to issue a stablecoin that Americans can buy, it has to screen against the U.S. sanctions list. You can't do both without choosing which set of rules governs your financial institutions.

The two systems

There are now two digital currency architectures being built on Earth at the same time.

The first is the American system. Private stablecoins, issued by licensed companies, regulated by Treasury and the OCC, backed by U.S. Treasuries, screened against the sanctions list. The Federal Reserve is banned by statute from issuing a competing digital dollar. The architecture is: private sector builds it, government licenses and monitors it, and the only way in is through the compliance stack.

The second is the BRICS system. Sovereign central bank digital currencies, issued by national governments, linked through bilateral or multilateral interoperability agreements, settling in local currencies, explicitly designed to reduce dependence on the dollar and bypass the U.S. correspondent banking system.

Both systems are real. Both are being built right now. The question is which countries end up inside which system and whether any country can be inside both.

The GENIUS Act rule gives the answer: you can be inside the American system only if you have a reciprocal arrangement with the United States. That arrangement requires your issuers to comply with U.S. law. Which means you can link your payment system to Russia's, or you can have your stablecoins sold to Americans. Doing both requires your institutions to follow two sets of rules that directly contradict each other because U.S. law requires screening Russian entities out of the system, and the BRICS linkage requires letting them in.

Why the bilateral deals are the key

The United States is not trying to ban BRICS currencies. It's not trying to stop other countries from building their own payment systems. It doesn't need to.

What it's doing is making the rules for the largest consumer market on earth and offering every country a choice: sign a deal with us, and your financial institutions get access to 330 million consumers and the deepest capital market in history. Don't sign, and your digital currency stops at our border.

That's not a threat. It's a sorting mechanism.

The bilateral trade deals currently being negotiated are not just about tariff rates on steel and soybeans. They are enrollment agreements for a monetary architecture. Every country that signs is opting into a system where its financial institutions must comply with American sanctions law, American anti-money-laundering requirements, and American lawful orders in exchange for access to the American market.

The trade deal is the financial deal is the digital currency deal. One negotiation. One signature. Three gates.

The bottom line

Sixty countries are negotiating bilateral agreements with the United States right now. Most of them think they're negotiating tariff rates.

They are also negotiating whether their banks can issue digital dollars. Whether their payment systems can reach American consumers. Whether their financial institutions are inside or outside the system that will govern how digital money moves for the next generation.

Nobody told them that. It's in the rule. Published today. https://t.co/HofC518DKu, press release SB0605.

Education Is Not Coaching

Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s announcement of free online coaching for competitive examinations may sound attractive—and free access to quality preparation is certainly welcome. But it cannot become a substitute for fixing India’s school education system.

The question raised in the accompanying video is therefore important: why is the solution being presented at the coaching stage when the foundations of education are built in schools?

A recent NITI Aayog analysis reported that the number of government schools fell from about 11.07 lakh in 2014–15 to 10.13 lakh in 2024–25—a decline of roughly 94,000. Government-school enrolment also fell substantially, while private-school numbers increased. The report points to demographic changes, declining enrolment and school consolidation as important factors.

So the issue is not simply that “94,000 schools were deliberately shut by one government.” Some schools were consolidated or merged because of very low enrolment. But that makes the central question even more important:

When a neighbourhood government school disappears, what happens to the child who depended on it?

And if public schooling is strong, adequately staffed and capable of providing quality learning, why should families have to spend enormous sums on private coaching merely to compete in examinations?

Free online coaching can help. But it addresses the symptom.

The deeper reform must begin much earlier:

Strong government schools → good teachers → foundational learning → critical thinking → fair examinations → less dependence on expensive coaching.

A tablet, an app or a free coaching portal cannot repair a weak classroom, an absent teacher, inadequate infrastructure or a child who has already fallen behind academically.

India does not merely need free coaching for competitive exams.

India needs quality public education that makes expensive coaching less necessary in the first place.

That is the real education reform.

text:
THE DRUG ROUTE INTO INDIA

A fact based investigation from Afghanistan and Pakistan to Punjab, from Myanmar to the Northeast, and from the border to India's streets

The Indian drug problem is often presented as a story about addicts.

That is the wrong place to begin.

The real story begins thousands of kilometres away, in places where opium is cultivated, synthetic drugs are manufactured, armed groups control territory, criminal organisations operate across borders and legitimate trade can be used to conceal illegal cargo.

By the time a packet of heroin reaches a young person in Punjab, or a tablet of methamphetamine reaches a college student in Kerala, the product may already have passed through several countries, several intermediaries, shell businesses, transport networks, financiers and local distributors.

India sits between two of the world's most important illicit drug producing regions.

To the west lies the Golden Crescent, centred historically on Afghanistan and extending through Pakistan and Iran.

To the east lies the Golden Triangle, centred on Myanmar, Laos and Thailand.

India shares a 3,323 kilometre border with Pakistan and a 1,643 kilometre border with Myanmar. It is therefore not simply a destination market. It can also become a transit country. 

And the nature of the threat is changing.

The old image of the Indian drug trade was largely heroin and opium. The newer picture contains methamphetamine, MDMA, LSD, cocaine, synthetic stimulants, pharmaceutical drugs and drugs ordered through encrypted communications and delivered through increasingly sophisticated logistics.

The most important question, therefore, is not whether India has a drug problem.

It does.

The question is what happens when two international drug corridors meet an enormous domestic market.

That is where this story begins.

---

CHAPTER ONE

THE GOLDEN CRESCENT

Afghanistan, Pakistan and the western route into India

For decades Afghanistan has been one of the world's principal sources of illicit opium.

The geography explains part of it. The politics explains another part. Decades of conflict weakened state control over remote areas, while opium provided farmers, traders and armed groups with a highly profitable commodity that could move across borders.

But there is an important fact that is sometimes missed in today's discussion.

Afghanistan's opium economy has changed dramatically since the Taliban announced its ban on poppy cultivation.

UNODC estimates that Afghanistan cultivated approximately 232,000 hectares of opium poppy in 2022. By 2025 that had fallen to approximately 10,200 hectares. Estimated opium production fell to 296 tonnes in 2025, down 32 percent from 2024 and dramatically below the pre ban period. UNODC estimated that the 2025 crop could produce approximately 22 to 34 tonnes of export quality heroin. 

That does not mean the Afghan drug threat disappeared.

Existing stocks remain.

Trafficking networks remain.

Processing and distribution networks remain.

And the trade has increasingly adapted.

The western drug corridor now has several important components.

Afghanistan remains a source of opiates.

Pakistan provides a major geographical corridor between Afghanistan and India.

Iran provides another major trafficking corridor and maritime route.

The Arabian Sea provides access to India's western coast.

The product can then move inland.

This is why the Indian authorities increasingly describe the western drug problem not simply as smuggling, but as an organised transnational network.

UNODC has noted that heroin traditionally entered South Asia through the India Pakistan land border, but that the pattern has changed. Iran became an important departure point for shipments identified by Indian authorities, with a substantial proportion entering India by sea. 

The western route therefore has multiple doors.

The land border is one.

text:
In 2025, an NIA case involving drone delivered explosives and arms resulted in convictions of nine accused. The investigation linked the operation to Pakistan based and Germany based terrorist handlers and the Khalistan Zindabad Force. 

That is why the term narco terrorism has entered India's security vocabulary.

It does not mean every drug smuggler is a terrorist.

It means that where criminal drug networks intersect with terrorist financing, weapons trafficking or terror organisations, the drug trade becomes a national security problem.

---

# CHAPTER FOUR

## THE INDIAN SIDE OF THE NETWORK

The international supplier is only one part of the machine.

Someone has to receive the consignment.

Someone has to store it.

Someone has to transport it.

Someone has to distribute it.

Someone has to collect the money.

Someone has to launder the proceeds.

And someone has to protect the network from detection.

This is where the Indian drug trade becomes more complicated.

The evidence from major investigations points to a layered structure rather than a single organisation.

At the top can be an overseas supplier or handler.

Below that can be an Indian receiver.

Then come transporters and warehouse operators.

Below them are local distributors.

At the bottom are street dealers and users.

The money moves in the opposite direction.

The drugs move down.

The money moves up.

The system can involve legitimate businesses, rented premises, bank accounts, properties and apparently ordinary commercial transactions.

The Mundra investigation exposed the use of shell import companies. The Attari investigation exposed the use of legitimate trade documentation, godowns, Indian entities, bank accounts, property purchases and hawala. 

There is another layer.

Officials themselves can sometimes become compromised.

In April 2025, Punjab Police arrested eight people in a Pakistan backed drug cartel investigation, including a DRI inspector, according to police. The investigation also identified Dubai based hawala operators. 

In another Punjab case in 2025, police arrested a head constable along with three employees of Punjab State Power Corporation Limited in a heroin trafficking investigation. 

These cases do not prove that government agencies as institutions are part of the drug trade.

They prove something more uncomfortable.

A large criminal economy can sometimes penetrate institutions designed to stop it.

That is the difference between corruption being an isolated crime and corruption becoming an enabling component of organised crime.

---

# CHAPTER FIVE

## POLITICS ENTERS THE PICTURE

This is the chapter where facts must be separated from political claims.

There is evidence of individual politicians and political workers becoming accused or arrested in drug related investigations.

There is not evidence sufficient to say that an entire political party is a drug trafficking organisation.

Those are completely different claims.

Punjab provides several examples.

Former Congress MLA Satkar Kaur, who later joined the BJP, was arrested by Punjab Police in October 2024 in a case involving alleged heroin supply. Police said 100 grams of heroin was recovered during a decoy operation. 

In 2025, Shiromani Akali Dal leader and former Punjab minister Bikram Singh Majithia was arrested in a disproportionate assets investigation arising from a drug case. Punjab Vigilance Bureau alleged that more than Rs 540 crore in drug money had been traced in the investigation. The allegations remain matters for the legal process and should not be treated as a conviction merely because an arrest occurred. 

In 2026, an AAP backed village sarpanch in Tarn Taran was arrested by NCB after investigators reported the seizure of 18 kilograms of heroin. 

[3 /n]
_source_value: illegal betting website blocked India police

text:
Another AAP local leader was arrested in Amritsar in 2026 in a case involving 4.3 kilograms of heroin and weapons, according to police reports. 

The pattern is more useful than the party labels.

Different political affiliations have appeared in different cases.

That tells us that the drug economy is not automatically loyal to one ideology.

It is loyal to money.

The same principle applies to the police.

Individual police officers have been arrested in drug cases.

That does not mean Punjab Police is part of the drug trade.

It means any system handling enormous quantities of illegal money is vulnerable to infiltration.

The correct response is therefore not to declare an entire political party, police force or government agency guilty.

The correct response is to follow the money, the communications, the properties, the bank accounts and the chain of custody until the evidence identifies the individuals involved.

That is precisely why financial investigations have become increasingly important.

---

# CHAPTER SIX

## THE SECOND FRONT

### Myanmar and the Golden Triangle

Now move east.

The geography changes.

The problem does not.

Myanmar sits at the centre of the Golden Triangle, historically one of the world's major opium producing regions.

But the Golden Triangle has undergone a major transformation.

Methamphetamine has become increasingly important.

UNODC describes the Golden Triangle as a major hub for both opium and synthetic drug production and says methamphetamine has become the dominant drug in seizure data in the region. Methamphetamine seizures in East and Southeast Asia increased substantially over the past decade. 

The heart of the problem is Shan State.

Remote terrain.

Weak governance.

Long running armed conflict.

Cross border trade.

Criminal networks.

Armed groups.

And enormous profits.

These conditions create an environment in which drug manufacturing and trafficking can survive even when governments conduct enforcement operations.

UNODC has reported that criminal organisations and armed groups in the Golden Triangle sometimes cooperate around illicit economies and that political instability and corruption in Myanmar, particularly in Shan State, have aggravated the problem. 

The important point is that this is not a simple story of one organisation manufacturing drugs.

It is an ecosystem.

Manufacturing networks.

Armed groups.

Traffickers.

Financial operators.

Transporters.

Corrupt intermediaries.

And international criminal organisations.

The exact participants can change.

The business model remains.

---

# CHAPTER SEVEN

## THE DRUGS COMING FROM MYANMAR

The principal concern for India's Northeast is heroin and methamphetamine.

Methamphetamine appears in different forms.

Yaba tablets are methamphetamine based tablets widely trafficked in the region.

Crystal methamphetamine is another form.

The Northeast is especially exposed because India shares a 1,643 kilometre border with Myanmar through Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Manipur and Mizoram. 

The problem is not theoretical.

UNODC has documented the westward movement of methamphetamine from Myanmar into South Asia.

Its 2025 regional synthetic drugs report noted that methamphetamine trafficking flows from Myanmar into northeastern Indian states continued in early 2025. The report also cited a Mizoram seizure of 236.44 kilograms of methamphetamine tablets in May 2025 and a seizure of 30.4 kilograms of methamphetamine tablets in Assam in April 2025. 

Myanmar's own production remains substantial.

UNODC estimated Myanmar's potential opium production at 995 tonnes in 2024. 

But the bigger strategic concern is the synthetic market.

Synthetic drugs do not depend on agricultural land in the same way as opium.

A laboratory can produce enormous quantities.

Production can move.

Precursors can move.

text:
Global Embarrassment

The government’s clumsy and ridiculous manner of “implementing” the Supreme Court’s order regarding Imran Khan’s health has brought disgrace and humiliation upon this government internationally.

The Supreme Court’s clear order was that Imran Khan should be taken to Shifa Hospital, where a medical board comprising Shifa’s doctors, in the presence of Imran’s personal physician and his sister, Dr. Uzma, would examine him, and that he would remain ostensibly there until September 16, when the court was to review the entire record.

At 12:23, Imran Khan was taken to PIMS Hospital, and at 5:00 he was declared healthy and sent back to jail.

This clearly demonstrates that the Shehbaz government was unwilling to comply with the Supreme Court’s order. Playing fast and loose with the law has long been the PML-N’s modus operandi—whether it was removing Junejo from the party presidency and creating the PML-N, the Memogate case, the attack on the judiciary, Nawaz Sharif’s platelet case, or the case of Imran Khan.

Had the government honestly implemented the Supreme Court’s decision, it would have deserved appreciation, political pressure would have eased, and an environment conducive to dialogue with the PTI would have emerged. But the PML-N leadership, blinded by its hatred for Imran Khan, appears determined to settle old scores.

Now condemnation is raining down from around the world.

And political tensions in the country will intensify further. So, whose bed will be rolled up next? Let us see. How long will the Field Marshal tolerate the stench of the hybrid system, when his office (CDSO) has, through an emergency amendment, been made autonomous from and superior to the Ministry of Defence, with sweeping powers?

It seems the Sharif Company has lost its bearings. It does not want PTI to settle its differences with the military. Yet Zulfi Bukhari, one of Imran Khan’s closest associates, welcomed the Supreme Court’s decision and had assured that there would be peaceful coexistence with the establishment.

Now the question is whether the Supreme Court will stand firm over its contempt, or whether the Shehbaz government will quietly retreat with its tail between its legs.

And if the PPP joins the Grand Opposition after the inclusion of Maulana Fazlur Rehman, who will save the PML-N’s lights from being extinguished, when the CDS office has become autonomous and beyond the Ministry of Defence, while the unemployed Defence Minister, Khawaja Asif, shamelessly sits outside the ministry’s door, crying over the same old grievances?

By Imtiaz Alam

text:
A Finnish parliamentarian has been blocked  from entering the UK to give an address on freedom of speech at a  conference this week, following her criminal conviction for “hate  speech” by Finland’s Supreme Court.

Longstanding Christian politician Päivi  Räsänen, who is a member of the Finnish Parliament’s “Friends of the  United Kingdom” group, was due to give a talk in person this week about  freedom of speech, at a religious freedom conference.

However, in July, Räsänen was informed  that her Electronic Travel Authorisation (ETA) to the UK had been  cancelled, despite her application initially being approved in June.

Räsänen will be forced to speak at the  event virtually on Wednesday and Friday, unless she is granted entry to  the country. The Finnish MP and ADF are now calling on the UK Home  Secretary Shabana Mahmood to make a last-minute intervention, to allow  Räsänen to attend in person on Friday.

This follows the Finnish grandmother and former Interior Minister’s “hate speech” conviction by  the Finnish Supreme Court in March 2026, for expressing her Christian  beliefs on marriage and human sexuality in a 2004 booklet written for  her church.

Räsänen’s criminal conviction was noted with concern by observers around the world, including the US State Department and the US Religious Liberty Commission, which was established by President Donald Trump.

Lutheran Bishop Juhana Pohjola, who was  criminally convicted alongside Räsänen for publishing her booklet, was  also blocked from entering the UK, after his ETA was denied in June.

After her ETA was cancelled, Räsänen  subsequently applied for a full visa and wrote to the UK Home Secretary  personally to ask that it be granted ahead of the conference this week.

To date, Räsänen has not received an  answer from the Home Secretary, and was informed that she would not be  given a response on her visa application in time to travel for the  event.

Räsänen, Bishop Pohjola and the Luther Foundation Finland, who were all convicted in March over Räsänen’s booklet, have appealed their  cases to the European Court of Human Rights, where they will be  represented by free speech legal advocacy organisation Alliance  Defending Freedom.

Räsänen said: “It is shocking that the  UK has blocked me, a democratically elected politician in an allied  European state, from entering the country.

“I was convicted of ‘hate speech’ in  Finland for peacefully expressing my Christian views. This was an  egregious case of state censorship, noted with concern by observers  around the world, including the US State Department and the US Religious  Liberty Commission.

“Even though this unjust conviction is  currently on appeal to the European Court of Human Rights, the UK has  likely refused me travel authorisation on this basis. In doing so, the  UK is punishing me for exercising my fundamental human rights.

“I call on Home Secretary Shabana  Mahmood to urgently intervene to allow me to enter the UK to speak at  this event. There is still time for this censorship to be reversed.”

Lorcán Price, legal counsel for Alliance  Defending Freedom, representing Räsänen, Bishop Pohjola and the Luther  Foundation Finland at the European Court of Human Rights, said: “In essence Päivi Räsänen has been blocked from entering the UK for peacefully expressing her Christian beliefs.

“This is not an isolated incident. The  UK has in the last year blocked a number of mainstream conservative  individuals, politicians, and now even a member of the Finnish  Parliament and a Lutheran bishop, from entering the country. This trend  is yet another example of the severe and escalating censorship crisis in  Great Britain.

“Furthermore, the British state is  increasingly cracking down on the rights of Christians in the UK:  Christians have been criminalised for silently praying, offering to  speak with people, publicly preaching their faith, and now they have  been blocked from entering the country for expressing their views.

“Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood should  act immediately to allow my client to enter the country, to speak in  person at the religious liberty event in Northern Ireland. Any further  silence on the Home Secretary’s part will reinforce to the British  people and observers around the world that this government has a  deep-seated antipathy to free speech.”

Bishop Pohjola said: “It is an Orwellian reality that I was blocked from entering the UK by the British state.

“For a senior Lutheran cleric to be  criminally sanctioned in one European country and blocked from entering  another, for merely publishing a church booklet which peacefully  expressed views the Finnish state disagreed with, is extremely alarming.

“It shows how far our civilisation has  strayed not only from its Christian roots, but even from respecting the  basic human rights of free speech and religious freedom. The two are  undoubtedly related, as a new secular orthodoxy has taken root across  Western countries, under which dissenters are punished harshly.

“I sincerely hope the UK Home  Secretary acts to allow Paivi to enter the country, and that the  European Court of Human Rights upholds our right to free speech.  Peacefully expressing views on marriage and human sexuality that  Christians have always held is not a crime.”

Background

The former Finnish Interior Minister,  medical doctor and grandmother of 12 was criminally prosecuted for  nearly seven years for sharing her Christian beliefs about marriage and  human sexuality in a 2019 tweet and live radio debate, as well as for  authoring a 2004 church booklet, for which she was charged alongside  Bishop Pohjola and the Luther Foundation Finland.

In 2021, Räsänen was formally charged with  “agitation against a minority group” under a section of the Finnish  criminal code titled “war crimes and crimes against humanity”.

Following unanimous acquittals on all  charges by two lower courts in 2022 and 2023, the state prosecutor  appealed again to the Finnish Supreme Court, regarding the tweet and  church booklet.

The case was heard in October 2025, and in  March 2026, in a narrow 3–2 decision, the Supreme Court upheld the  acquittal for the Bible verse tweet, but convicted Räsänen,  Bishop Pohjola and the Luther Foundation Finland for the 2004 booklet.  The radio show charge was not appealed to the Supreme Court, so that  acquittal stands.

The Supreme Court convicted Räsänen under  a law that was introduced years after the booklet was published, and  did so despite the court’s admission that the booklet “did not contain  incitement to violence or comparable threat-like fomenting of hatred”.

Christian Finnish Parliamentarian Blocked From Entering UK To Discuss Free Speech At Religious Liberty Conference

In an alarming display of censorship, the  Supreme Court fined Räsänen, Bishop Pohjola, and the Luther Foundation  Finland several thousand euros each, and ruled that the condemned  statements within the booklet must be “removed from public access and  destroyed”.

The US State Department commented on  Räsänen’s criminal prosecution, prior to her conviction in March: “In a  democracy, no one should face trial for peacefully sharing their  beliefs. The case against Finnish MP Päivi Räsänen, which accuses her of  hate speech for simply posting a Bible verse, is baseless, as two  courts have unanimously found.”

Following her conviction, the U.S. Embassy Finland said:  “A troubling ruling for religious freedom and freedom of expression:  Finland’s Supreme Court dismissed the charge over MP Päivi Räsänen’s  2019 Bible-verse social-media post, but convicted her over separate  passages in a Christian pamphlet and imposed a fine. Whatever one thinks  of the underlying views, the imposition of criminal liability for  nonviolent religious expression sets a troubling precedent for religious  freedom and freedom of expression.”

🚨 BREAKING: Government of India Orders Immediate Takedown of Dhruv Rathee’s (@dhruv_rathee)  Video.

The Grievance Appellate Committee (GAC), Ministry of Electronics & IT, Government of India, has passed an Order dated 15 July 2026 (Appeal No. 8321/2026) directing YouTube to remove the video titled “Can Hindus Eat Beef? | Kerala Story 2 Exposed” within 24 hours of receiving the Order.

Note: Although the order is dated 15.07.2026, it has been uploaded today (19 July 2026).

- The video contains deliberate and malicious statements insulting Bhagwan Shri Ram, Bhagwan Shri Krishna, and Sita Devi.

- It falsely claims they consumed meat (including deer meat) and alcohol, using distorted references from scriptures.

- Such content hurts the religious sentiments of crores of Hindus and is against societal harmony.

- YouTube’s arguments on “free speech” were not accepted. Freedom of expression comes with reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

The order was issued after Hon'ble Delhi High Court’s direction on 3rd July 2026 to decide the appeal within 15 days.

Important: This observation and finding by the GAC that the video hurts religious sentiments will also have a strong bearing on the decision of the Ld. Magistrate before whom our petition seeking registration of FIR against Dhruv Rathee is pending for hearing on 10.09.2026.

Faith cannot be mocked under the garb of “content creation.” Justice is being delivered step by step.

UPDATE TO ALL MEMBERS ON LOCUM ENGAGEMENT & CASUALIZATION

The leadership of NARD, ably led by the Strategic P-MUS (Garkuwan Matasan Arewa), is pleased to update members on the outcome of the FMoHSW Committee on  Regulation and Casualization of Doctors.

Following extensive consultations, the Committee has developed a National Policy on the Engagement of Locum, aimed at ensuring fair, transparent and non-exploitative engagement of temporary healthcare personnel.

KEY RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Recruitment & Approval:
   Locum engagement must be based on a clearly identified staffing gap and approved by the appropriate hospital authorities.

2. Contract Duration:
   Initial locum contracts shall not exceed 6 months, with only one additional 6-month renewal permitted. Continuous engagement for 12 months makes the position eligible for permanent appointment.

3. Maximum Work Hours:
   Healthcare personnel shall work a maximum of 48 hours per week, including weekends. Excess hours must be appropriately compensated.

4. Maximum Duty Period:
   No healthcare personnel shall work beyond 24 continuous hours, including call duty.

5. Mandatory Rest:
   
   - Minimum 12 hours between shifts.

   - Mandatory 24-hour post-call rest after weekday and weekend calls.

   - A 1-hour break after 6 hours of continuous work.

6. Call Duty:
   
   - Maximum 2 calls per week.

   - Maximum 1 weekend call per month.

   - Calls must be equitably distributed.

7. Remuneration & Welfare:
Pay rates are standardized in alignment with the government's 
Scheme of Service. Remuneration must be paid monthly without delay, accompanied by monthly 
payslips. 

Locum staff are entitled to all government-approved leaves, public holidays, and occupational insurance coverage.

8. Excess Work Hours:
   Excess hours must be properly documented, monitored and adequately compensated, or appropriately balanced with structured time-off.

9. Protection Against Abuse:
   Locum engagement must not be used as a permanent substitute for substantive recruitment or as a means of exploiting healthcare workers.

10. Integration & Safety: All locum workers must undergo mandatory orientation and integration into their respective clinical or administrative teams. Institutions are required to provide safe 
working environment, adequate call rooms, refreshments during prolonged calls/shifts, and burnout prevention programs.

11. Discipline & Grievance Process: Professional misconduct shall be governed by the regulatory 
council guidelines. Contracts can be terminated by either party with a one-month notice or payment in lieu, and all accrued entitlements must be settled within 14 days of termination. Disputes escalate through institutional mechanisms up to the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, and the Federal Ministry of Labour and Employment.

12. Monitoring: The Ministry would ensure Institutions do not engage in exploitative staffing practices and violations of this guideline in line with the Nigerian Labour Law.

13. Policy Review and Effective Date:
This policy becomes legally binding on the exact date of approval by the Federal Ministry of 
Health and Social Welfare (FMoH&SW). To ensure its continuous operational relevance, the 
policy mandates a comprehensive evaluation and review within two (2) years of its 
implementation.

The policy is expected to provide a more structured and equitable framework for locum engagement across Nigerian health institutions.

Appreciation to the Hon. Coordinating Minister for Health and Social Welfare, Prof. Mohammad Ali Pate for this approval.

Special appreciation to the Hon. Minister of State for Health and Social Welfare, Dr. Iziak Adekunle Salako for his guidance and dictation to seeing this through.

Appreciations are also in order to our distinguished NARDites in the Committee for a job well done. Thank you Dr. Kwarshak Kevin Yakubu, the VP 2 of NARD. Thank you Dr. Shuaibu Ibrahim, the Secretary General of NARD.

NARD is particularly proud of this accomplishments and proves once again what we can achieve when we come together as a team.

NARD remains committed to protecting the dignity, welfare, rights and professional interests of every Nigerian doctor.

It is our hope that the National Council on Health will also give their stamp of approval on this.

Dr. Abdulmajid Yahya Ibrahim
NARD PSS
